title: Images on surfaces
subtitle: UVs, sampling, and color that stays correct.

lessons.title: Wrap an image around a mesh
body: A texture is an image sampled by a material. UV coordinates tell each part of a surface which part of that image to use. U and V usually range from 0 to 1 across an image.
Built-in geometries already provide UVs. We draw a checkerboard on a tiny canvas so this example works without an external image. Assign the texture to material.map and the sphere will display it.
lessons.hint: Replace material.map = null with material.map = texture.

quiz.question: What do UV coordinates describe?
quiz.explanation: UVs map a location on a surface to a location in an image.

lessons.title: Tile a texture
body: A texture normally clamps its edges when UVs go outside its bounds. RepeatWrapping instead repeats the image. Enable it separately along U and V with wrapS and wrapT.
texture.repeat scales how many times the image tiles over the existing UV range. Repetition changes sampling; it does not add geometry or require a larger source image.
lessons.hint: Both wrapping modes are already RepeatWrapping. Edit texture.repeat.set(1, 1).

quiz.question: Which wrapping mode tiles an image?
quiz.explanation: RepeatWrapping repeats samples when texture coordinates cross an image boundary.

lessons.title: Keep your colors honest
body: Lighting calculations use linear color values. Most images painted for display, including our checkerboard, contain sRGB colors. The texture’s colorSpace tells Three.js how to interpret those values.

Color textures normally need SRGBColorSpace. Data textures such as normal, roughness, or metalness maps normally keep NoColorSpace. The renderer converts its linear result to the output color space; do not add a second manual conversion.
lessons.task: Mark this color texture as THREE.SRGBColorSpace.
lessons.hint: Change texture.colorSpace from NoColorSpace to SRGBColorSpace.

quiz.question: Which texture usually contains sRGB color?
quiz.explanation: Base-color images represent display colors; normal and roughness maps contain numerical data.

lessons.title: Crisp pixels or soft samples?
body: A texture rarely lines up exactly with screen pixels. Filters decide how its samples are combined when displayed larger or smaller than the original image.

Linear filtering blends neighboring samples. Nearest filtering chooses the closest sample, giving a crisp pixel-art look. Minification often uses mipmaps: prefiltered smaller versions that reduce shimmering when textures shrink into the distance.
lessons.hint: The magnification filter controls the look when the texture is enlarged.

quiz.question: What does nearest filtering avoid?
quiz.explanation: Nearest sampling preserves hard pixel edges, though it can still alias.

lessons.title: Detail without more polygons
body: A bump map uses height-like data to perturb a surface’s shading normal. It creates the impression of small ridges without changing the actual mesh silhouette.

Normal maps directly encode directions and serve a similar purpose. Both are data rather than display color. Our checkerboard becomes a simple bump pattern. Increase bumpScale to make the lighting change more obvious, then inspect the unchanged outline.
lessons.hint: The same canvas is used as data here, so colorSpace remains NoColorSpace.

quiz.question: Does a bump map change a mesh’s silhouette?
quiz.explanation: Bump mapping changes lighting normals; displacement or geometry changes are needed to alter the silhouette.
